lesson.title: Python CLI automation and structured logging
lesson.why: A script becomes dependable automation when callers can predict its inputs, outputs and failure behavior. Structured logs make individual operations diagnosable without scraping human prose or leaking the credentials used by the process.
lesson.what: A Python command-line tool parses arguments, validates them, performs bounded work and returns a meaningful exit status. Keep machine-readable results separate from diagnostic events, and attach enough context to correlate failures with their operation.

concepts.name: CLI contracts
concepts.body: Argparse provides help, typed conversion and usage errors. Validate ranges and relationships after parsing: an integer is not necessarily a valid retry count. Document defaults so unattended callers do not depend on changing implicit behavior.

concepts.name: Output channels
concepts.body: Use stdout for the requested result and stderr for diagnostics. A JSON consumer cannot parse output reliably if progress messages appear between JSON records. Exit zero signals the defined success condition; nonzero statuses distinguish failures according to the tool's documented contract.

concepts.name: Structured events
concepts.body: JSON log fields such as event, operation_id, duration_ms and outcome support searching without fragile string matching. Logging formatters must actually serialize JSON; passing a dictionary to ordinary logging does not automatically produce valid JSON output.

concepts.name: Safe failure handling
concepts.body: Catch errors where useful context or recovery is possible, not simply to hide tracebacks and return success. Set deadlines for external work and redact sensitive values. Logs should record what failed without including access tokens, private payloads or unbounded response bodies.

e2e: Parse explicit arguments and reject invalid values before any side effect.
Create an operation identifier and start a bounded unit of work.
Emit structured diagnostic events to stderr and the result to stdout.
Return a documented exit status and preserve enough nonsecret evidence for a retry decision.

tasks.name: Emit a JSON result
steps: Run `python -c "import json; print(json.dumps({'count': 3, 'ok': True}, sort_keys=True))"`. Expected output is a JSON object with count 3 and ok true. Notice JSON's lowercase boolean rather than Python's True representation.

tasks.name: Specify CLI validation
steps: Design a fictional --attempts argument accepting integers from one through five. Write expected outcomes for 3, 0 and apple: accepted, range error and parse error. Require failures before file writes or requests; a parsed integer alone is insufficient validation.

tasks.name: Design a log event
steps: Write a synthetic event with operation_id demo-1, event import_finished, records 3 and duration_ms 12. Mark these numbers illustrative, not measured. Exclude request authorization and full source records, retaining only the context needed to diagnose this import.

tasks.name: Define a failure contract
steps: A fictional input file is missing. Specify no result on stdout, a redacted input_missing event on stderr and a documented nonzero exit code. Explain why printing an error and exiting zero would mislead a scheduler into marking the job complete.

key_terms: CLI: command-line interface.
Exit status: numeric process outcome.
Structured log: event with machine-readable fields.
Correlation ID: identifier joining related operation events.
lesson.safety: Run only the supplied local serialization command. Do not log credentials or connect this exercise to production files or APIs.
cleanup: The command creates no files; discard synthetic event notes if no longer needed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical automation returns valid JSON sometimes but fails when verbose logging is enabled. What would you inspect?
interview_points: Separate stdout results from stderr diagnostics.
Verify actual JSON serialization and stable schemas.
Check documented exit statuses.
Redact sensitive data while retaining operation context.

automation/python-cli-automation-and-str.core: Validate CLI values before side effects. Reserve stdout for results and stderr for diagnostics. Serialize structured events deliberately, use bounded work and return truthful documented exit statuses without exposing secrets.
objectives: Design machine-readable output and error contracts.
prerequisites: Have Python 3 and understand functions and exceptions.

storyboard.title: Progress output corrupts a JSON consumer
storyboard.objective: Explain why result and diagnostic channels must remain separate.

scenes.title: Result contract
scenes.caption: The caller expects one documented JSON result.
scenes.narration: The CLI validates arguments and prepares its result, while diagnostic context belongs on the separate error stream.

scenes.title: Mixed streams break parsing
scenes.caption: A human progress line is not part of the result schema.
scenes.narration: Verbose progress is printed to standard output. The JSON consumer fails even though the requested calculation completed successfully.

scenes.title: Separate and serialize
scenes.caption: Keep logs structured and result output clean.
scenes.narration: The tool serializes the result on standard output, writes redacted events to standard error and returns the documented exit status.

lesson.title: Bash robust scripts and exit handling
lesson.why: Shell scripts combine commands whose failures and argument parsing can be subtle. Explicit checks, quoting and scoped cleanup prevent a failed prerequisite from being hidden behind a successful final echo or an accidental wildcard expansion.
lesson.what: Robust Bash automation defines its input contract, quotes data, checks important statuses and limits side effects. Shell options can help, but their context-dependent behavior does not replace reasoning about each operation's expected failures.

concepts.name: Arguments are data
concepts.body: Double-quote expansions that represent a single argument and use arrays for argument lists. Word splitting and globbing can turn one user value into multiple operands. Avoid eval for constructing commands from input because it reinterprets data as shell syntax.

concepts.name: Explicit exit handling
concepts.body: Test important commands with if or a deliberate status capture. Set -e has exceptions in conditions and compound constructs, so it is not a universal exception mechanism. Distinguish expected no-result statuses from actual operational failure.

concepts.name: Pipelines and subshells
concepts.body: Pipefail helps expose upstream errors, while pipeline elements often run in subshells. Variables assigned inside a piped loop may not survive afterward. Choose process substitution or another explicit input method when state must remain in the current Bash process.

concepts.name: Cleanup and interruption
concepts.body: Traps can arrange bounded cleanup on normal exit or signals, but SIGKILL cannot be handled. Track exactly which resources the script created. Cleanup must not delete an unvalidated path or overwrite the original failure status with its own unrelated result.

e2e: Validate required arguments and construct command arguments without string evaluation.
Run prerequisites and branch explicitly on their expected success and failure statuses.
Perform scoped work while tracking only resources owned by this invocation.
Run safe cleanup and return the original meaningful outcome to the caller.

tasks.name: Preserve one argument
steps: In Bash run `value='two words'; printf '<%s>\n' "$value"`. Expect one line `<two words>`. Compare unquoted expansion only on paper and explain how it can become two arguments; never test this with filenames or destructive commands.

tasks.name: Expose failure without errexit
steps: Run `if false; then printf 'ok\n'; else printf 'failed\n'; fi`. Expected output is failed. Explain why the script intentionally handles this status rather than assuming a shell option will always terminate at the right point.

tasks.name: Compare pipeline outcomes
steps: Run `bash -o pipefail -c 'false | true; printf "%s\n" "$?"'`. Expect 1 because the earlier command failed. Contrast the ordinary last-command status of zero, and explain why expected grep no-match needs a separate branch.

tasks.name: Review cleanup ownership
steps: A fictional script receives an empty directory argument and plans recursive deletion on exit. Reject that design. Specify a newly created disposable directory, validated ownership, explicit filenames and preservation of the work command's status; no deletion needs to run here.

key_terms: Expansion: shell transformation of argument text.
Trap: handler for selected shell events.
Subshell: child shell execution context.
Pipefail: pipeline status policy exposing earlier failure.
lesson.safety: Run only supplied no-write commands. Do not use eval, recursive cleanup or privileged operations with external input.
cleanup: No files or background processes are created; the child Bash invocation changes no persistent shell options.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical script uses set -e but continues after an error inside a condition. Is that necessarily a Bash bug?
interview_points: Explain errexit's context-dependent exceptions.
Use explicit checks around important operations.
Preserve meaningful exit statuses.
Quote data and scope cleanup independently of error options.

automation/bash-robust-scripts-and-exit-.core: Quote data and use argument arrays instead of eval. Explicitly handle important statuses; errexit is context-dependent. Use pipefail deliberately and track cleanup ownership without deleting unvalidated paths or masking the original error.
objectives: Explain quoting and explicit exit decisions.
Design scoped cleanup without unsafe path assumptions.
prerequisites: Have Bash and understand command exit statuses.

storyboard.title: The final command hides an earlier failure
storyboard.objective: Trace shell status through a pipeline.

scenes.title: Commands compose
scenes.caption: The scheduler depends on a truthful final outcome.
scenes.narration: A prerequisite feeds a later command. The scheduler can react correctly only if the script reports failures that matter.

scenes.title: Earlier failure is hidden
scenes.caption: The final command succeeds despite missing input.
scenes.narration: The prerequisite fails but the final command returns zero. Ordinary last-command status makes the entire operation appear successful.

scenes.title: Handle expected statuses explicitly
scenes.caption: Pipefail and deliberate branches preserve the real result.
scenes.narration: The script checks upstream failure, handles expected empty results separately and returns a meaningful nonzero outcome without unsafe cleanup.

lesson.title: PowerShell objects pipelines and automation
lesson.why: PowerShell pipelines usually carry typed objects, not the text shown on screen. Preserving those objects makes automation resilient to display changes and enables accurate filtering without fragile parsing of formatted tables.
lesson.what: Cmdlets produce objects with properties and methods. The pipeline binds these objects to receiving commands. Formatting, serialization and error behavior are separate concerns that must be controlled when building unattended PowerShell workflows.

concepts.name: Objects versus display
concepts.body: Select-Object projects properties, while Format-Table creates formatting instructions for display. Formatting midway through a data pipeline destroys the original data shape for later consumers. Inspect members and property values rather than splitting aligned terminal output into columns.

concepts.name: Filtering and enumeration
concepts.body: Where-Object selects objects using property expressions and ForEach-Object transforms each incoming item. Pipeline enumeration can make zero, one and many results behave differently when collected. Use explicit array collection where callers require a stable countable sequence.

concepts.name: Errors and native commands
concepts.body: Some cmdlet errors are nonterminating and do not enter catch unless promoted with ErrorAction Stop. Native programs report process statuses through LASTEXITCODE; their behavior is not identical to cmdlet exceptions. Check the relevant channel instead of assuming one universal error model.

concepts.name: Safe mutation and serialization
concepts.body: Cmdlets supporting ShouldProcess can expose WhatIf previews, but not every command implements them. JSON conversion has depth and type considerations. Prefer explicit property selection and sufficiently deep serialization over assuming displayed output captures a complete nested object.

e2e: Create or retrieve typed objects and inspect their expected properties.
Filter and transform objects without applying display formatting prematurely.
Perform approved actions with the command's actual error and preview semantics.
Serialize selected results or format only at the final human-display boundary.

tasks.name: Filter synthetic objects
steps: Run `$items = @([pscustomobject]@{Name='api';Count=3},[pscustomobject]@{Name='worker';Count=1}); $items | Where-Object Count -gt 1 | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name`. Expected output is api. No system processes or files are modified.

tasks.name: Compare projection and formatting
steps: Using the same synthetic objects, compare `$items | Select-Object Name,Count | ConvertTo-Json` with a paper pipeline that inserts Format-Table before serialization. Explain why formatting records are not equivalent to the original Name and Count data.

tasks.name: Plan error handling
steps: A fictional file-reading cmdlet reports a nonterminating error inside try. Specify ErrorAction Stop when the failure must reach catch. For a native tool, separately inspect LASTEXITCODE and document success codes; do not claim that try alone catches every failure.

tasks.name: Review a preview promise
steps: A proposed automation appends -WhatIf to every command, including an arbitrary native executable. Reject the assumption. Check documented ShouldProcess support and use a synthetic input or explicit planning mode where preview is unavailable, before permitting any real side effect.

key_terms: Cmdlet: PowerShell command with structured binding.
Property: named value on an object.
Terminating error: failure that interrupts normal execution.
ShouldProcess: PowerShell action-confirmation and preview mechanism.
lesson.safety: Use only synthetic objects. Do not enumerate sensitive host data or invoke real account, file-removal or cloud commands.
cleanup: Remove the optional local variables with `Remove-Variable items -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`; no persistent state was created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical PowerShell script converts a formatted table to JSON and loses its expected properties. What should change?
interview_points: Keep original objects until serialization.
Use Select-Object for projection, not Format-Table.
Format only for final human display.
Handle cmdlet errors and native exit codes deliberately.

automation/powershell-objects-pipelines-.core: PowerShell pipelines carry objects. Project with Select-Object and format only at the display boundary. ErrorAction Stop governs catchable cmdlet failures; native exit codes need separate checks. WhatIf is safe only where actually supported.
prerequisites: Have PowerShell and understand properties and arrays.

storyboard.title: Formatting turns data into display instructions
storyboard.objective: Keep objects intact until the output boundary.

scenes.title: Typed records enter
scenes.caption: Properties support direct filtering and projection.
scenes.narration: The pipeline receives objects with Name and Count properties, allowing comparisons without parsing their terminal appearance.

scenes.title: Premature formatting
scenes.caption: Display instructions replace the expected data objects.
scenes.narration: Format-Table is inserted before serialization. The consumer now receives formatting information rather than the original business properties.

scenes.title: Move formatting to the end
scenes.caption: Serialize selected objects, not the displayed table.
scenes.narration: The script retains typed objects through filtering and projection, serializes them directly and reserves formatting for a separate human-facing output.

lesson.title: REST APIs pagination retries and rate limits
lesson.why: A successful first page is not a complete export, and a retry can repeat a side effect. Reliable API clients preserve pagination state, honor limits and treat response loss as an ambiguous outcome rather than permission to resend blindly.
lesson.what: REST-style APIs expose resources through HTTP contracts. Pagination splits collections; rate limits constrain request volume. Robust clients need bounded deadlines, documented retry decisions and explicit handling for changing collections and partial progress.

concepts.name: Pagination contracts
concepts.body: Follow the server's documented next link or opaque cursor until no continuation remains. Do not invent cursor values or assume a short page always means completion. Offset pagination can skip or duplicate items when the collection changes during traversal.

concepts.name: Retry classification
concepts.body: Some transient failures merit retry, while validation and authorization failures usually require correction. A timeout after a write may mean the write succeeded. Use the API's idempotency mechanism or reconciliation endpoint rather than assuming every POST can be safely replayed.

concepts.name: Backoff and deadlines
concepts.body: Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries and avoids synchronized bursts. Retry-After can express seconds or an HTTP date. Honor documented guidance within an overall deadline and maximum attempts, accounting for request duration as well as waiting time.

concepts.name: Checkpoints and limits
concepts.body: Persist progress only after safely processing a page or record according to the destination's atomicity rules. Track rate budgets and request identifiers without logging credentials. Bounded concurrency protects both the client and service; more workers can increase throttling rather than throughput.

e2e: Issue an authenticated request through the approved client contract with a deadline.
Validate the response and process its records without assuming the collection is complete.
Checkpoint completed work and follow the provided continuation when present.
On transient failure, apply bounded safe retry or reconciliation, then resume without duplicate effects.

tasks.name: Walk opaque cursors
steps: Use fictional pages: first records [a,b] with next c1, second [c] with next c2, third [d] without next. Expected export is a,b,c,d. The one-record second page is not completion because its continuation still exists.

tasks.name: Calculate retry waiting
steps: A policy waits one, two and four seconds before three retries. Waiting totals seven seconds, excluding request time; four total attempts occur including the first. Explain why a five-second overall deadline cannot allow the full sequence unchanged.

tasks.name: Handle throttling
steps: A hypothetical response is 429 with Retry-After: 3. Plan to wait at least the instructed interval if the deadline permits, reduce concurrency and avoid simultaneous client retries. Do not contact an actual API to provoke throttling.

tasks.name: Recover an ambiguous write
steps: An order POST times out after the service may have committed. Reuse its documented idempotency key or query status by the original operation ID. If neither exists, escalate reconciliation instead of inventing a new ID and repeating the purchase.

key_terms: Cursor: opaque pagination continuation token.
429: HTTP too-many-requests response.
Jitter: randomized retry delay component.
Checkpoint: durable record of completed progress.
lesson.safety: Use fictional HTTP records only. Do not call production APIs, collect credentials or generate intentional rate-limit traffic.
cleanup: Discard synthetic cursors and request identifiers; no external requests or persisted checkpoints were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical export misses records and creates duplicates after timeouts. Which client assumptions would you inspect?
interview_points: Follow explicit continuation rather than page-size guesses.
Review changing-collection semantics and checkpoints.
Separate read retries from ambiguous write recovery.
Bound attempts and honor rate-limit guidance.

automation/rest-apis-pagination-retries-.core: Follow server continuations to completion. Retry only when semantics permit, with jitter, limits and an overall deadline. Checkpoint completed effects and reconcile ambiguous writes using stable identifiers; never log authentication values.
objectives: Calculate bounded retry behavior and write recovery.
prerequisites: Understand HTTP methods, status codes and JSON records.

storyboard.title: A short page still has a continuation
storyboard.objective: Trace complete pagination with safe retry state.

scenes.title: First page processed
scenes.caption: The next cursor identifies more work.
scenes.narration: The client processes the first page and records completed work before requesting the server-provided continuation.

scenes.title: Short-page mistake
scenes.caption: Page size alone does not determine completion.
scenes.narration: The second page contains one record and another cursor. Stopping because it is short would omit the final page.

scenes.title: Continue until absent
scenes.caption: Preserve progress and follow the actual contract.
scenes.narration: The client follows the remaining cursor and completes only when the continuation is absent, using bounded retries without duplicating completed effects.

lesson.title: JSON YAML configuration and schema validation
lesson.why: A configuration file can parse successfully yet contain a dangerous value or misspelled field. Schema and semantic validation move mistakes to a predictable preflight stage instead of discovering them after partial infrastructure or application changes.
lesson.what: JSON and YAML serialize structured data; neither automatically defines an application's allowed configuration. Validation should check syntax, types, required fields, ranges and cross-field meaning while handling secrets and parser differences deliberately.

concepts.name: Syntax and data types
concepts.body: JSON has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null with strict quoting rules. YAML adds syntax conveniences and parser-dependent scalar interpretation. Quote ambiguous values and use the application's actual parser rather than assuming every YAML implementation resolves them identically.

concepts.name: Schema boundaries
concepts.body: A schema can require fields, reject unknown properties and limit values. Closed schemas catch misspellings such as retrise instead of retries. Decide intentionally whether forward-compatible unknown fields are allowed; silently ignoring them can conceal a user's intended safety control.

concepts.name: Semantic checks
concepts.body: Type correctness is not business correctness. A timeout of zero may be an integer but violate requirements; a retry delay may exceed the overall deadline. Validate relationships and units after parsing, before any side effect.

concepts.name: Safe loading and secrets
concepts.body: Use safe YAML loading modes that do not instantiate arbitrary language objects. Reject duplicate keys where supported because overwritten values can confuse reviewers. Store secret references rather than values, and redact diagnostics so a validation error does not expose an entire sensitive document.

e2e: Read a bounded configuration document with the expected parser and safe loading mode.
Reject malformed syntax, duplicate-key ambiguity and unsupported structure.
Validate required properties, types, ranges and cross-field constraints.
Produce a redacted plan and perform side effects only after all validation passes.

tasks.name: Parse a known JSON object
steps: Start a Python 3 REPL with `python`, then enter `import json; x=json.loads('{"retries":3,"enabled":true}'); print(type(x['retries']).__name__, type(x['enabled']).__name__)`. Expect `int bool`. Run this code inside Python, not the shell, to avoid shell-specific quoting. Exit with `exit()`. No files are read or written; parsing alone provides no schema guarantee.

tasks.name: Find an unknown field
tasks.goal: Catch intent hidden by a typo.
steps: A fictional schema permits retries and timeout_seconds, but input contains retrise: 3. Under a closed schema the expected outcome is rejection naming the unknown field. Explain why ignoring it could fall back to an unintended retry default.

tasks.name: Validate relationships
steps: Given timeout_seconds=10, attempts=3 and deadline_seconds=20, the worst-case attempt time alone is 30 seconds before backoff. Reject or revise this plan even though every field is an integer. Document whether deadlines bound the entire operation or each attempt.

tasks.name: Review YAML safely
steps: On paper, create two identical timeout keys with different values and an unquoted value that might be interpreted as a boolean by some parsers. Require duplicate-key rejection and explicit quoting or typed validation, using the application's supported parser rather than executing custom YAML tags.

key_terms: Schema: allowed data structure and constraints.
Scalar: individual primitive value.
Semantic validation: checking meaning and relationships.
Duplicate key: repeated mapping name with ambiguous intent.
lesson.safety: Use supplied synthetic JSON only. Do not load untrusted custom YAML tags or paste secrets into validators.
cleanup: The local parse creates no files; retain only the synthetic schema decisions.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical configuration parser accepts every file but deployments fail when a timeout key is misspelled. What validation is missing?
interview_points: Parsing does not enforce the application schema.
Reject unknown fields and require intended properties.
Check ranges, units and cross-field deadlines.
Report errors without exposing secret values.

automation/json-yaml-configuration-and-s.core: Parse safely, then validate structure and meaning. Reject unknown or duplicate keys where the contract requires it. Check units and cross-field constraints before side effects; keep secret references and redacted errors separate from values.
objectives: Distinguish parsing, schema and semantic validation.
prerequisites: Have Python 3 and understand dictionaries and primitive types.

storyboard.title: Valid JSON can still violate the configuration contract
storyboard.objective: Place schema checks before operational side effects.

scenes.title: Syntax passes
scenes.caption: The document becomes an object, not an approved plan.
scenes.narration: The parser accepts a syntactically valid object containing retry and timeout settings. Their names and relationships still need validation.

scenes.title: Typo or deadline conflict
scenes.caption: Unknown keys and incompatible values must not reach execution.
scenes.narration: The validator finds a misspelled key or attempts exceeding the overall deadline, despite every value being valid JSON.

scenes.title: Correct before execution
scenes.caption: Only a fully validated configuration is actionable.
scenes.narration: The author fixes the contract violations, and the runner receives a validated configuration with redacted diagnostics rather than partial side effects.

lesson.title: Idempotent automation and transactional workflows
lesson.why: Automation is often retried after a crash or lost response. Without stable operation identity and carefully placed checkpoints, a retry can duplicate records, send the same notification twice or leave a partially completed workflow that looks successful.
lesson.what: Idempotent operations preserve the intended effect across repetition. Transactions make a defined set of changes atomic within one system. Multi-system workflows need explicit state, compensations or reconciliation because local atomicity does not automatically cross network boundaries.

concepts.name: Desired state
concepts.body: Compare observed state with the desired outcome and apply only necessary changes. Creating a directory if absent is different from appending the same line on every run. Idempotency concerns the effect, not simply whether the command exits successfully twice.

concepts.name: Atomic checkpoints
concepts.body: Record an operation identifier and business effect in the same transaction where possible. If the effect commits before the checkpoint, a crash can cause duplicate work on retry. If the checkpoint precedes the effect, a crash can cause skipped work.

concepts.name: Concurrency control
concepts.body: Two workers can both observe absence and race to create the same resource. Use unique constraints, conditional updates or compare-and-swap rather than a separate check alone. Locks need scoped ownership and failure handling; a stale lock must not block progress forever.

concepts.name: Compensation and reconciliation
concepts.body: A saga coordinates local steps with compensating actions when later steps fail. Compensation is not always a perfect inverse: an email cannot be unsent. Reconciliation compares recorded intent with actual external state and repairs gaps under a documented policy.

e2e: Assign a stable operation identifier and validate the desired end state.
Apply the local effect with its deduplication or version check atomically.
Advance workflow state only after confirmed progress and handle ambiguous remote outcomes.
Retry safely or compensate and reconcile, retaining evidence of incomplete work.

tasks.name: Predict repeated effects
steps: Offline, start with an empty set and add item demo-4 three times: expected membership contains one item. Contrast incrementing a counter three times, which produces three. Explain why an exit-zero result alone says nothing about whether either effect is repeat-safe.

tasks.name: Locate the crash window
steps: A worker debits 10, crashes and never records completion. On retry it debits again. Move debit and operation-ID insertion into one hypothetical database transaction with a unique ID; repeated demo-4 should return the recorded result, not another debit.

tasks.name: Resolve a concurrent create
steps: Two workers both read that username demo-user is absent. Expected safe outcome with a unique constraint is one insert and one conflict to handle. Explain why checking first without a constraint cannot guarantee uniqueness under concurrent execution.

tasks.name: Design a compensating workflow
steps: A fictional workflow reserves inventory then fails payment authorization. Define reservation release as compensation, with its own retryable identifier. If release fails, leave a visible reconciliation state rather than marking the whole operation complete or pretending the notification can be unsent.

key_terms: Idempotency: repetition preserves the intended effect.
Transaction: atomic unit within a defined system.
Compare-and-swap: conditional update against an expected version.
Compensation: action addressing an earlier completed step.
lesson.safety: Use paper ledgers only. Do not replay real purchases, payments, messages or provisioning requests.
cleanup: Keep the synthetic state diagram and remove fictional reservations from the worksheet; no external effects occurred.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical job checks whether a record exists before inserting it, yet duplicates appear during parallel runs. Why?
interview_points: The check and insert are separate raceable operations.
Enforce uniqueness or conditional atomic writes.
Use stable operation identifiers for retries.
Track partial external effects and reconcile them explicitly.

automation/idempotent-automation-and-tra.core: Repeat-safe effects need stable identity and atomic deduplication boundaries. Check-then-act is unsafe under concurrency. Use constraints or conditional updates; multi-system work requires visible state, compensation and reconciliation rather than assumed global transactions.
objectives: Design safe concurrent and compensating workflow behavior.
prerequisites: Understand database writes, retries and process crashes.

storyboard.title: A crash between effect and checkpoint duplicates work
storyboard.objective: Place deduplication with the business transaction.

scenes.title: Effect executes
scenes.caption: The operation changes business state.
scenes.narration: The worker debits the ledger. If completion is recorded separately, there is a crash window after the effect but before its checkpoint.

scenes.title: Retry repeats an unrecorded effect
scenes.caption: Missing completion is not proof that no work occurred.
scenes.narration: The worker crashes in that window and retries. Without atomic deduplication, the same intended operation can debit the ledger again.

scenes.title: Commit effect and identity together
scenes.caption: A repeat returns the stored result.
scenes.narration: The ledger commits the effect and unique operation record in one transaction, allowing retries to find the original result safely.

lesson.title: Unit integration contract and end-to-end testing
lesson.why: Different tests answer different questions. Thousands of isolated passing assertions cannot prove that two services agree on a payload, while relying only on a slow end-to-end suite makes failures expensive to locate and easy to ignore.
lesson.what: A test strategy layers focused component behavior, real dependency interaction, interface compatibility and complete user workflows. Choose each layer for the risk it detects, with deterministic fixtures, clear failure evidence and safe isolation.

concepts.name: Unit boundaries
concepts.body: Unit tests exercise a small behavior with controlled dependencies. They are fast and useful for edge cases, but excessive mocking can encode assumptions that differ from reality. Assert observable behavior rather than internal call order unless that order is the contract.

concepts.name: Integration evidence
concepts.body: Integration tests exercise actual boundaries such as database constraints, serialization or filesystem behavior. Use isolated fixtures and cleanup owned by the test. A realistic dependency can reveal transaction or encoding errors that a mock will never reproduce.

concepts.name: Contract compatibility
concepts.body: Contract tests check that producers and consumers agree on fields, types and behavior. They can catch a renamed field before deployment without executing every user journey. A compatible schema alone still cannot prove correct business meaning or authorization.

concepts.name: End-to-end confidence
concepts.body: End-to-end tests follow critical workflows through deployed components. They provide broad confidence but usually run slower and fail for more environmental reasons. Quarantine flaky tests with ownership and repair deadlines; automatic reruns must not disguise a consistently unreliable signal.

e2e: Identify a behavior risk and choose the narrowest test layer that can reveal it.
Create deterministic synthetic fixtures and isolate external effects.
Run assertions with enough context to distinguish product defects from environment failures.
Clean up owned resources and combine layered evidence without claiming unexecuted tests passed.

tasks.name: Run a tiny unit assertion
tasks.goal: Observe an exact local test outcome.
steps: Run `python -c "assert sum([2, 3]) == 5; print('unit example passed')"`. Expect unit example passed. This demonstrates assertion mechanics only; it is not evidence that any real application or production dependency has been tested.

tasks.name: Assign the right layer
tasks.goal: Match a defect to useful evidence.
steps: Classify three fictional risks: discount arithmetic, a database uniqueness constraint and checkout across services. Choose unit, integration and end-to-end respectively. Add a contract test for a renamed payment-response field to distinguish interface compatibility from complete checkout behavior.

tasks.name: Design a contract check
steps: A consumer requires integer total_cents but the producer proposes string total. Define a fixture and expected rejection before deployment. Explain why a producer-only unit test accepting its own new payload would not reveal that the existing consumer still expects the old field.

tasks.name: Handle flaky evidence
tasks.goal: Repair signal quality rather than hide failures.
steps: A hypothetical test fails one run in ten due to a shared clock assumption. Record the pattern, replace uncontrolled time with an explicit clock fixture where appropriate and verify the underlying behavior. Do not claim nine passing runs cancel the failure.

key_terms: Fixture: controlled test input or environment.
Unit test: focused behavior check.
Contract test: interface agreement check.
Flake: inconsistent result without a relevant intended change.
lesson.safety: Use local assertions and synthetic fixtures only. Do not run tests against production accounts or send real purchases or notifications.
cleanup: The supplied assertion creates no files; any future fixtures must clean up only resources created by their own test run.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical service passes unit tests but breaks consumers after renaming a response field. Which missing evidence would you add?
interview_points: Add producer-consumer contract checks.
Retain focused unit tests for local logic.
Use integration tests for real serialization boundaries.
Verify critical user journeys without relying only on a slow broad suite.

automation/unit-integration-contract-and.core: Use unit tests for focused behavior, integration tests for real boundaries, contracts for interface compatibility and end-to-end tests for critical journeys. Control fixtures and time, clean up owned effects and report only executed evidence.
objectives: Select test layers based on failure risk.
prerequisites: Have Python 3 and understand functions and service interfaces.

storyboard.title: Producer unit tests miss a consumer contract break
storyboard.objective: Show where interface compatibility needs separate evidence.

scenes.title: Existing agreement
scenes.caption: The consumer expects an integer total_cents field.
scenes.narration: The producer and consumer share a documented response contract, which a focused compatibility check can verify with synthetic payloads.

scenes.title: Producer changes alone
scenes.caption: Its own unit tests may accept the new field.
scenes.narration: The producer renames the field and updates its local tests. Those passing tests do not exercise the older consumer's expectation.

scenes.title: Contract catches the mismatch
scenes.caption: Reject or migrate the incompatible interface before rollout.
scenes.narration: The contract check rejects the incompatible payload, prompting a backward-compatible transition and targeted integration evidence before deployment.
